slides.title: doctest
slides.main: If the code changes but the example doesn't, the test fails: docs stop lying.

body.text:
import doctest

def square(x):
    """Square a number.

    >>> square(3)
    9
    >>> square(-2)
    4
    """
    return x * x

runner = doctest.DocTestRunner(verbose=False)
for t in doctest.DocTestFinder().find(square, "square", globs={"square": square}):
    runner.run(t)
print(runner.summarize(verbose=False))
ON SCREEN
TestResults(failed=0, attempted=2)
From the terminal: python -m doctest file.py.

slides.title: Code that is easy to test
slides.main: Pass time, network, files in: faking is trivial, no mock needed.

body.text:
from datetime import datetime

def greeting(now):               # time is a parameter, not a call inside
    return "Good morning" if now.hour < 12 else "Good afternoon"

assert greeting(datetime(2024, 1, 1, 9)) == "Good morning"
assert greeting(datetime(2024, 1, 1, 15)) == "Good afternoon"
print("testable without a clock or a mock")
ON SCREEN
testable without a clock or a mock

slides.title: Properties and random tests
slides.main: A fixed seed makes a random test reproducible: replay any failing case.

body.text:
import random

random.seed(1)
for _ in range(1000):
    xs = [random.randint(-50, 50) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 20))]
    s = sorted(xs)
    assert all(a <= b for a, b in zip(s, s[1:]))
    assert len(s) == len(xs) and sorted(s) == s
print("sorting properties hold on 1000 random inputs")
ON SCREEN
sorting properties hold on 1000 random inputs
Line coverage is a guide, not a goal: 100% doesn't prove correctness.

slides.title: Common mistakes
slides.main: A test should be small, fast, about one idea, and independent of its neighbors.

body.text: ON SCREEN
True ['a']
Run test_b alone and it fails. Also: too many checks per test, no isolation from time and network, weakening a test instead of fixing code.
